sections.h2: Running load, peak load and monthly units: what each number is for
p: The 3,017 W running load of the default home is what an inverter, UPS or generator must carry for as long as everything is on, and what the main breaker sees. The 4,881 W peak is the moment the largest motor or compressor starts on top of that load: it sets the surge rating of an inverter and, more often than the running load, the size of a generator.

The 458 units a month are a different quantity: energy, not power. They are what the bill charges for and what a solar system has to produce. Take the running and peak watts to the inverter size calculator or the generator size calculator, and the daily units to the solar system size calculator.

The sanctioned load printed on the bill is the kW the DISCO agreed to supply to the house. Enter it and this calculator compares the running load with it: the third worked example, with a non-inverter AC and a geyser, runs at 272% of a 2 kW sanctioned load. A running load close to or above the sanctioned load is the usual reason a home is told to apply for a load extension before adding an AC or solar.

Not everything in a house runs at once, so the sanctioned load to apply for is worked out from the connected load with a diversity factor. The sanctioned load calculator does that, and the load check before adding an AC shows whether one more AC fits the connection you have.

sections.h2: Home load in amps and the wiring
p: At 230 V and a power factor of 0.8, the default running load of 3,017 W is 15.4 A on a single-phase supply. That is the current the main cable and the main breaker carry when everything on the list is running.

Each circuit in the house carries only its own share, so wire and breaker sizes are chosen circuit by circuit. Use the home wiring load schedule to size every circuit at once, or the MCB size calculator for one circuit; have a licensed electrician confirm the main breaker and cable before changing them.

faq.q: How do I calculate the electrical load of my house?
faq.a: List every appliance that can run at the same time, take the running watts from its label or the appliance list, multiply by how many you have and add them up. Divide the total by volts × power factor (230 V × 0.8 in Pakistan) for amps.

faq.q: What is the total load of a house in kW?
faq.a: Most Pakistani homes without an AC run at well under one kilowatt; a home with one inverter AC, fans, lights and a fridge runs at about 3 kW, and each extra inverter AC adds about 1 kW on average and more at full speed.

faq.q: What is a connected load and how is it different from running load?
faq.a: Connected load is the sum of everything wired in the house; running load is what is on at the same moment. Bills and sanctioned loads are set against expected demand, so the running load is the number to plan with.

faq.q: How many units does this load use per month?
faq.a: Each appliance's watts × hours a day ÷ 1,000 gives its units a day; add them and multiply by 30.42. The default home above uses about 15.1 units a day and 458 a month.

faq.q: Can I use this load to size a UPS, inverter or solar system?
faq.a: Yes. The running watts are the continuous rating your inverter or UPS needs (plus a safety margin), the peak watts are its surge rating, and the daily units are what a solar system must produce. The next-step links below take your numbers to those calculators.

faq.q: What is the electrical load estimation for a new house?
faq.a: Add the rooms' lights and fans, one AC per bedroom you plan to cool, the kitchen appliances and the water pump, then apply a diversity factor because not everything runs together; the sanctioned-load calculator does this and recommends the kW to apply for.

key_facts: Home electrical load in watts = the sum of the running watts of every appliance that is on at the same time; divide by volts × power factor to get amps.
Peak load adds the starting surge of the largest motor or compressor only once, because two motors rarely start in the same instant.
Monthly units (kWh) = watts × hours a day ÷ 1,000 × 30.42 days, added over every appliance; this is the number your electricity bill is based on.
The default example home above (18 appliances of 6 kinds) draws 3,017 W running, 4,881 W at peak and uses about 458 units a month.
mistakes: Adding every appliance in the house. Only count what runs at the same time; an iron used for half an hour matters for the monthly units but rarely for the peak load.

Using the AC's rated input as its average draw. An inverter AC's input varies with the room temperature; the watts here are a planning average, and the rated maximum is used for wire and breaker sizing.
Ignoring starting surge. A non-inverter AC or a water pump draws about three times its running watts for a second or two, which is what trips an undersized breaker or inverter.
Confusing watts with units. Watts are the rate of use right now; units (kWh) are watts × hours ÷ 1,000 and are what the bill charges for.

how.tpl: Running load = the watts of every appliance × its quantity, added up = {{out.running_w|int}} W. Peak load adds the starting surge of the largest motor = {{out.peak_w|int}} W. Current = {{out.running_w|int}} W ÷ ({{out.volts}} V × {{out.pf|2}} power factor) = {{out.amps|1}} A. Energy = each appliance's watts × hours a day (an inverter AC counts at its average draw, below its rated watts), added up = {{out.daily_kwh|1}} units a day, × {{out.days|2}} days = {{out.monthly_units|int}} units a month. Bill: energy {{out.bill_calc}} = {{out.bill_energy_rs|rs}}, plus the fixed charge {{out.bill_fixed}}, FC surcharge, QTA and GST (no FPA, {{out.bill_tariff}}) = {{out.monthly_rs|rs}} a month, the same as the electricity bill calculator gives for these units.
how.text: Running load = the watts of every appliance × its quantity, added up = 3,017 W. Peak load adds the starting surge of the largest motor = 4,881 W. Current = 3,017 W ÷ (230 V × 0.85 power factor) = 15.4 A. Energy = each appliance's watts × hours a day (an inverter AC counts at its average draw, below its rated watts), added up = 15.1 units a day, × 30.42 days = 458 units a month. Bill: energy 458.34 × Rs 38.95 = Rs 17,852, plus the fixed charge for 1 kW, FC surcharge, QTA and GST (no FPA, unprotected) = Rs 23,402 a month, the same as the electricity bill calculator gives for these units.

legal.t: This is an estimate, not an official bill. Your DISCO's bill and NEPRA's tariff notifications are the official figures. Do not use this result as evidence before a court, NEPRA, the Wafaqi Mohtasib or any other forum. To dispute a bill, complain to your DISCO first, using the complaint number printed on your bill, then file a NEPRA complaint or a Wafaqi Mohtasib complaint.

msg.inverter_ac_no_payback: At these figures the saving is too small to pay back the extra price within the working life of an air conditioner. Check the hours a year, the tariff and both power figures.

msg.tou_required_at_5kw: Connections of 5 kW or more use a Time-of-Use meter: see the ToU bill link under Sanctioned load.
msg.protected_at_tou: Protected and lifeline rates do not apply at 5 kW sanctioned load or more (a Time-of-Use meter). Untick the box.
msg.ac_protected_lost: With the AC your monthly total goes over the protected limit, so this bill and the bills of the following six months are charged at unprotected rates. Fewer AC hours may keep you protected.
msg.ac_above_sanctioned: This AC alone is above your sanctioned load: apply for a higher one before installing it.
msg.period_unknown: We do not have the QTA rate for that quarter. Enter the QTA from your bill.
msg.appliance_unknown: Pick an appliance from the list, or choose Custom and enter its watts.
msg.other_start_below_run: Starting watts of the other loads cannot be lower than their running watts.
msg.tou_peak_estimate: At 5 kW sanctioned load or more the import is billed on Time-of-Use rates, and the peak units are our estimate (a share of the import, see how it works). Enter the peak units from your ToU bill for your own figure.
msg.tou_bill_estimate: At 5 kW sanctioned load or more the bill is on Time-of-Use rates, and the peak units are our estimate (a share of all units, see how it works). Enter the peak units from your ToU bill under Advanced for your own figure.
msg.tou_share_estimate: At 5 kW sanctioned load or more the bill is on Time-of-Use rates, with our estimate of the share of units used in the peak hours (see how it works). For your own peak units, use the electricity bill calculator.
msg.above_standard_sizes: This is above the largest standard size we list. Split the array or circuit into two, or ask a licensed electrician or engineer; the sizes shown are the calculated minimums.
msg.generator_above_standard_sizes: This is above the largest generator size we list. Use two generators on separate circuits or a larger industrial set, and ask a licensed electrician; the size shown is the calculated minimum.
msg.forecast_unavailable: The live forecast is not available right now, so a typical day is shown. Try again later.
msg.hours_year_invalid: Hours a year must be above 0 and at most 8,760.
msg.duty_invalid: Compressor on-time must be a share from 0 to 1, e.g. 0.8.
msg.typical_used: Blank boxes in your list use the typical value for that appliance (its listed watts and hours a day, quantity 1). Type your own numbers for an exact result.
msg.internal_non_finite: These numbers are outside a realistic range. Please check your inputs.

examples.title: Small home: 4 kinds of appliance, no AC
examples.text: Three fans, eight LED bulbs, a TV and a fridge total 611 W running and 1,611 W when the fridge compressor starts, which is 3.3 A at 230 V. They use about 5.4 units a day and 163 units a month, within a 1 kW sanctioned load.

examples.title: Family home with two inverter ACs
examples.text: Five fans, twelve bulbs, a fridge, two 1.5 ton inverter ACs, an iron and a water pump come to 5,496 W running and 7,360 W at peak, or 27 A. Expect about 739 units a month, an estimated bill of Rs 47,167 at the Rs 47.20 slab, using 137% of a 4 kW sanctioned load.

examples.title: Non-inverter AC plus an electric geyser on a 2 kW connection
examples.text: The running load is 5,440 W, but the non-inverter compressor pushes the peak to 9,040 W, or 43.7 A for a moment. At 272% of the sanctioned load this connection is overloaded; a higher sanctioned load or an inverter AC is the fix.

content.answer: A typical home with 18 appliances running together (fans, lights, a fridge, a TV, a 1.5 ton inverter AC and a water pump) draws about 3,017 W, or 15.4 A at 230 V, and uses about 458 units a month. Add your own appliances below to get your total watts, peak load, amps and monthly units.

formula.text: P = Σ (W × qty); I = P ÷ (V × PF); units/day = Σ (W × qty × h) ÷ 1000
lines: P = total running load in watts
W = running watts of one appliance, qty = how many
I = current in amps, V = supply voltage, PF = power factor
h = hours a day the appliance runs
Peak = P + the largest (starting watts − running watts) of any motor

content.safety: If the running load is close to your sanctioned load or your main breaker rating, do not add more; ask your DISCO for a higher sanctioned load and have a licensed electrician check the main cable and breaker.
